utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a few more questions. On the 15th, 16th of April, on the night, where were you? Remind me.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CALIC
utterances.text: I was in the cinema building. I was not on duty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is your evidence that you have no idea what happened on the night of the 15th, 16th; no idea of any preparations for an attack? Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CALIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, what did you learn of the attack that was mounted that following morning?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CALIC
utterances.text: I did not learn anything. I saw everything in the morning, around 5.30 in the morning, when the shelling of the town began. At first I did not know what was being shelled and where, which part of town was being shelled. Then we were given orders to go to the elementary school building. I already said that. We were supposed to cover a clearing that went from the direction of Stari Vitez, Mahala, to the secondary school and the elementary school building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By "clearing," you mean clearing of Muslims?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CALIC
utterances.text: No. I'm speaking about a clearing, an area that is clear, open.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were the Brigade Military Police, apart from yourself, doing on the night of the 15th, 16th, please?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CALIC
utterances.text: We were on duty, securing the command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, we know -- I needn't trouble you with the document. It's 671.5. It went in last week -- that by 2.50 on the 16th of April, there were 50 Muslims in the cellar of the brigade police station. Can you explain how they got there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CALIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. At that time, I wasn't down there; I was at the school, so I can't say anything about that to you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You saw Cerkez in the cinema complex on the night of the 15th, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CALIC
utterances.text: I couldn't really remember who are all the people I saw at headquarters. I can't. I can't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your memory better when you spoke to people in 1998 in America?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CALIC
utterances.text: I don't know. These are certain periods of time, and I can't really give you an exact answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have previous criminal convictions in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CALIC
utterances.text: Criminal proceedings were instituted against me, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In respect to what criminal offences?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CALIC
utterances.text: Serious bodily injury with death as a consequence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you decline to reveal those details to the American authorities when you obtained permission to go and live there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CALIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you saying you told them all about it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CALIC
utterances.text: They didn't ask me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. Just a few more questions. You were involved, then, until August in the detention of people in Vitez, would that be correct, or later than August?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CALIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were involved in guarding, in detaining people against their will in Vitez right away from April of 1993 until the summer or the autumn, October.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CALIC
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You guarded individuals, did you not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CALIC
utterances.text: I did not guard any individuals. This was a larger group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware, and I'm going to try and take this very quickly but I want your answers, please; were you aware of people being kept in the building where Kovac had his office, and indeed, were you aware of a woman being kept in Kovac's office?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CALIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear any complaints by a woman who'd been detained, of being raped?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CALIC
utterances.text: I don't know about any woman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you accept that people were taken to dig trenches under compulsion and under guard?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CALIC
utterances.text: They went. There were cases of people going to dig trenches. I already said that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as you explained to the people who spoke to you in 1998, would this be right, Cerkez never did anything to stop the use of people for those purposes.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CALIC
utterances.text: I don't know how much Mr. Cerkez knew in respect of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is the answer to my question that, to your knowledge, Mr. Cerkez did nothing to stop the use of people for those purposes?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CALIC
utterances.text: I am not aware of anything in this regard as to whether anyone did anything. I complained to Mr. Borislav Jozic a few times, and he said that he would make an effort to stop this because it was in violation of some kind of convention or something.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm dealing with matters quickly. I'm not necessarily accepting topics. I am coming to the very last question I want to ask him unless I'm told by my colleagues there's something I've missed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you saying, about Dr. Mujezinovic, that you were the person who collected him the night the fighting broke out? I'm sorry, on the 19th, some days later?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CALIC
utterances.text: I don't know which day it was. It wasn't during the night. It was during the day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But as you understood it, was this the first time that Dr. Mujezinovic had been approached and taken in and approached for whatever purpose?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CALIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you go alone or with anyone else?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CALIC
utterances.text: I went alone from the outpatient office, together with -- after having talked to Dr. Tibold.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see, he has told us of being taken by two people, Anto Kovac, known as Zabac, and Ratko Nuk, on the occasion he was taken to negotiate matters, amongst other things. What you are speaking about isn't that occasion, is it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CALIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I only know about the case when I went to ask the gentleman to come to the medical centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And certainly you didn't go with these two other people, Kovac and Nuk.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CALIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Just a couple of questions, Your Honour. Re-examined by Mr. Mikulicic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Calic, my colleague, the Prosecutor, asked you whether Mr. Cerkez did anything to stop people from being taken away to trench digging. You said that you were not aware of that. I'm going to ask you something slightly different but on the same subject. In view of your experience, including your professional experience as a member of the military police, did Mr. Cerkez have the possibility and the authority to issue such orders?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CALIC
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Also you were asked about your previous criminal record, if any. Was there ever a legal decision that was passed by which you were actually found guilty of having committed a crime?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CALIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Calic, that concludes your evidence. You are now free to go. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kovacic, you said you wanted a quarter of an hour; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually, we took advantage of the break that we had. We talked, so I can communicate our position to you now. Irrespective of the decision passed by the Trial Chamber, and we appreciate that the fact that it could have helped, in fact, we have been brought into an impossible position due to the conduct of the Prosecution in respect of the discovery of documents. My professional obligation does not allow me to advise my client to testify under such conditions nor can my client do that without knowing the contents of the new evidence, although they will not be used in the cross-examination or will be used but only up to a point, but obviously these documents do exist. I just wish to add yet another reason. It is not the Defence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You cannot challenge the Ruling of the Trial Chamber, if that is what you are seeking to do. What are you going to do, Mr. Kovacic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am certainly not challenging the Ruling of the Trial Chamber. I just wish to present the reasons why we cannot accept this. On the contrary --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, Mr. Kovacic. It's not a question of your accepting it or not. It's a Ruling, so you are bound by it. Now, what are you trying to say? It's the time now for, if you wish to, to call Mr. Cerkez. The decision whether to call him or not is entirely yours and his together. We have refused the application for an adjournment. We are not going to review that now. We've considered all the matters and given our reasons. If you are going to call him, call him. If not, don't try and use the decision of the Trial Chamber as an excuse, if that's what you're going to do. It sounds as though -- I may be wrong -- but that sounds as though that's what you are trying to do and that would be wholly wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, by no means do I intend to challenge in any way your Ruling. On the contrary, we think that your Ruling has put us in a better position compared to the position that we were in before that. However, I just feel duty-bound to tell the Court, at least as a matter of courtesy, that we have been brought into a new position due to the fact that the Prosecution has piled a heap of documents on us. In some way it is being implied by the Prosecution that the Defence is involved in some kind of conspiracy that could have received these documents and manipulated with them or something like that. We were not even close to these documents, and I think I mentioned this before. We got the first documents in Croatia after the Prosecutor did, after the Prosecutor paved the way for us, and we actually thank him for it. There is only one thing that I wanted to say to the Trial Chamber in order to make our position better understood. In spite of these better conditions that have been provided for us, we believe that we are profession duty-bound to advise our client not to testify since he has not seen the new documents. The documents have not been tendered yet, but they will and might be tendered in due time, so we would like to thank you and, of course, we are glad to answer any questions you might have, if any.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So I take it you are closing your case, subject to production of exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that is correct. We are closing our case. We don't have any further witnesses. There is only one open witness which we earlier mentioned, linguistic witness. Unfortunately, there is not, so far, any agreement with the Prosecution on that issue. We will simply give up, but if the Court will allow us to bring that witness on rebuttal, perhaps we will appreciate that. If not, not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I just want to consult. There are various administrative matters which we've got to deal with. There's the question of rebuttal. So we will need to sit, I guess, for at least one more day this week. I'll hear any submissions that anybody else has got to make about things. Just one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: In order not to waste time, what we need to do is to consider the outstanding matters and anything else which usefully can be done this week. What we have in mind is, since we are not going to sit till 3.00, is to spend some time in discussing ourselves what remains to be done and, if it's convenient, to sit again at 3.30. If the parties would also like to consider the position as to when it might be convenient to deal with all the outstanding issues, to deal with as much as we can this week. It may be helpful at 3.30 to make a list of the things and then decide when we're going to deal with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I agree. I think I can help the Chamber. I don't think the transcript is going to be a problem, that is, the Cerkez transcript witnesses, not so far as we're concerned. I'll confirm that. As to rebuttal, the argument was originally timetabled for Friday, and I'll find out when we'll be ready to deal with that. Obviously, Thursday might be easier. But on the other hand, the interests of the Chamber and its members might be in favour of having it on Wednesday or even earlier, if we can manage it. So I'll review that. There is one short matter that I'd like to deal with in closed session. Perhaps I can deal with that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.30 p.m. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The first matter I'm going to deal with is to give a ng in relation to a video recording, Exhibit Z1428. This was to be admitted in the case in the -- during the evidence of Witness DL. Objection was taken on the ground that that witness did not appear although, in fact, it wasn't certain whether he did or not, and the Trial Chamber agreed that it would look at the video to determine whether he did or not. A further objection was taken that the events shown were outside the period of the indictment. However, the Trial Chamber have determined, one, that Witness DL does indeed appear, the subject matter being a visit of President Tudjman, and DL is quite clear, as is the accused Mr. Kordic, who appears. In the view of the Trial Chamber, it's a relevant matter although it's slightly after the time in the indictment and, therefore, it is admissible. However, there is part of the recording which deals with totally different matters and not the visit, and that will be deleted. That deals with that matter. We have considered what is outstanding, and we find the following matters have to be resolved this week before Thursday: First of all, the rebuttal witnesses, the extent to be permitted involving, too, the disclosure of three witnesses. The next matter is the objections, if any, to the Kordic Defence exhibits, which is being resolved. The Cerkez expert witness, Ms. Nikolic-Hoyt. The Prosecution video of the scene, which we have to see. The Cerkez transcript witnesses and the order of cross-examination of the Court witnesses are all matters on which rulings may be necessary and, if they are to be given, they should be dealt with. There may be other matters. The Chamber would have in mind dealing with these matters on Wednesday or Thursday. We'll hear the parties on that and make a decision. It would seem that there is at least half a day's work there, maybe more, but in any event, it can be contained within the day. Any submissions?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I help? I think, actually, a number of the issues won't take particularly long, although, for example, looking at the list of matters, as to the Cerkez transcript witnesses, although the evidence that they give is not evidence with which we agree or which we accept, and although the cross-examination in the other case in which they were called was not necessarily on the points that we would have cross-examined on ourselves, we take the view, subject to any different view of the Chamber, that for what that material may be worth in due course, it being largely cumulative, we don't object to any of them going before you. So we hope that that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you, we'll admit those.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As to Nikolic-Hoyt, as I understand Mr. Kovacic this morning, he was effectively abandoning her for the time being and just leaving open as a possibility calling her at rejoinder stage. We, in any event, were minded to argue that the evidence is tangential in the extreme, and that the point that seems to be -- that Mr. Kovacic wants in is the point that he and Mr. Naumovski have made whenever they speak to a witness and say to the witness, "We speak the same language," and the witness accepts it. That point is noncontroversial so far as we are concerned and the way they deal with it. There may be other aspects of the imposition of the use of the Croatian language which have been given in evidence and which are relevant, but the particular point to which this evidence seems to be going seems to be tangential and, in any event, is reserved at best or worst for rejoinder. So I expect that issue may have gone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me hear Mr. Kovacic on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I agree that it is indeed really not a very important thing. But, however, there is a claim in paragraph 4, if I am not wrong, I think it is 4 in introductory part of the indictment that, among other things, based on the fact that Croatians in Bosnia were using Croatian language, it is like a good base to conclude that Republic of Croatia, if I may say, controlled that war. On such a claim, I offered a witness expert who basically said what language was spoken in all that country, at that time the same country. We did hear the testimony about that also used, if you would probably remember, a witness Anto Miketa who explained what were the subjects in the school and books, et cetera, and I agree it is peripheral but there is such a claim in the indictment and that was the only idea about this expert testimony. For technical reasons, unfortunately, this lady is not able to come, and the only technical possibility to avoid video conference which is, I understood from the registry, very expensive, it was merely a suggestion as an exception to have that testimony during the rejoinder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So what are you asking us to do with that now, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I would like to have at least an open possibility to call that expert witness during the rejoinder but not really as a rejoinder witness because she certainly is not rejoinder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. That does not have to be dealt with, then. That still leaves the rebuttal, which may or may not be a substantial issue, and the Kordic Defence exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I help with Kordic Defence exhibits? There have been two meetings, I think, last week involving both sides and registry, and there's been a very substantial boiling down to a reduced mass what are outstanding as issues between the parties, and we've been in the process of preparing really rather a short document reflecting what's in dispute. Over the period between this morning's hearing and today, I think further items have been deleted by further consideration given to the topics. There is the potential for unresolved questions about certain exhibits because a large number of exhibits, I think all Blaskic orders, have yet to be translated, but the reality is that if they are Blaskic orders on their face, there's going to be no grounds for objecting to them. And providing we can technically keep open any objection in relation to any particular exhibit that turns up, I think we'll be able to lodge a very short document, or pretty short document, which won't take you very long to dispose of, either on Wednesday or Thursday. As to Blaskic orders and their provenance and so on, there is one of the ones, as I explained already, I think this morning, that I've referred to -- specifically to Mr. Kovacic. I haven't yet to Mr. Sayers, but I did to Mr. Kovacic because of the prospect of evidence today, explaining that we do now -- we will now be arguing that that document is not a genuine document as to its purported date, and we have more material on that. The Chamber may remember that document of the 15th of June -- 15th of April. But that apart, I think the Blaskic orders, by and large, will be admissible -- I beg your pardon. It's up to the Chamber whether they are admitted or not. They won't be objected to by us. And the remaining issues, probably less than half an hour, 20 minutes to resolve, I would have thought.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The video.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The video, I'm hoping that it's going to be made tomorrow. I've asked -- well, I've asked for it to be kept as short as is reasonably possible, while it's still going to be useful and of interest. It covers, of course, not only locations that we wanted to cover, but also those that Mr. Kovacic wanted to cover. And we, I think, managed to find all, or all but about one or two, of the locations he asked us to film. I think that its duration is likely to be, but this is very much a guess at the moment, 40 minutes or thereabouts, and I'm very hopeful that it will be available for the witness to answer questions about it on Wednesday. I can't promise Wednesday, but I would hope Wednesday. And as to rebuttal, we would, I think, be happy to deal with it on either Wednesday or Thursday. I know that Mr. Sayers was going to provide an argument on Wednesday. It may be that with a court day off tomorrow, he'll be able to provide it a little earlier than that, but it's a matter for him and the Chamber really.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. President, with the day off tomorrow, we should be able to provide our submission on the rebuttal witnesses and the rebuttal exhibits. We'll do our best to get that polished up and in a professional form and filed as early as possible tomorrow so that it would be available, if the Court wishes, for argument on Wednesday. On the matter of exhibits, my information from the Registrar is that we now have all translations of all Croatian documents. They've already been submitted. And I think that all of the formal matters regarding authenticity, legibility, things of that variety, those have already been worked out, so the argument on Mr. Kordic's outstanding exhibits should be short. With respect to the video, obviously we weren't invited to participate in that process, and we would appreciate receiving a copy of it so that we can review it before it is considered for admission into evidence. There are a couple of issues that we would wish to discuss in private session, but that can be left for Wednesday. And I notice that there has been -- that the Court has recently entered an order requiring additional secret witnesses to be disclosed to us by Friday. We would appreciate it if the Court could accelerate the date for disclosure to the date when the rebuttal conference is going to be heard. The date of disclosure had originally been ordered to be the rebuttal conference on Friday. If it's going to be held on Wednesday, we would greatly appreciate it if we could know the identity of these last few witnesses on that day. And I think that's all the matters that we have, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So far as those are concerned, the position may differ as between them. One in particular, it may be one for whom we would apply for extension until at least Friday, for reasons that I can deal with probably on Wednesday. I'm not sure about the position as to the other two. I'll make inquiries as soon as we rise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The sooner they're disclosed, the better.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Of course, yes. Absolutely. I'm happy to say that the last transcript in respect of the (redacted) in B/C/S has now been provided, so that's an exercise that's been completed. We were served this morning with one affidavit by the Cerkez case that I don't think is shown as relating to any witness, and it may be there's now no longer any request to put the affidavit in. I don't know what the position is on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. It was just automatic work. In the eve of the Cerkez testimony we filed that affidavit, but now it does not fit into the Rule now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice, I'm speaking on behalf of the Chamber. The Chamber has just read the document entitled -- [In English] [inaudible] concerning rebuttal case. [Interpretation] We were surprised, because you are telling us that this list of rebuttal witnesses can vary from 12 to 25 or 13 to 25, and you said that you would probably call only 12 to 13 witnesses, but you had this list of 25 potential witnesses. Obviously, we want to have a clear idea, a definite idea on Wednesday or Thursday about the list of witnesses you intend to call as far as the rebuttal procedure, and we want a definite list. We also want to hear your submissions about the justification for calling these rebuttal witnesses with regard to the ongoing procedure. As we've explained, you have to explain why you call people in rebuttal, mentioning, for example, new exhibits, et cetera. That's what we are expecting from you on Wednesday or Thursday; i.e., we want to be something very definite, once and for all, thus enabling us to organise the end of the trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Two points. One, I think -- I'm afraid I haven't actually got the document with me. I foolishly didn't bring it down. But I think that you'll find that the document discriminates between two potential categories of witness. Notwithstanding the decision of the Appeals Chamber, it seems to us there is proper scope for admitting evidence by way of affidavit, and that argument will be addressed on Wednesday or Thursday, and they're identified in the schedule that accompanies the pleading as witnesses whose evidence might properly be accepted in that form. Thus I think the explanation for the difference in numbers. Second, I think that the schedule also identifies the subject matter of the witnesses, and thus the reason why they qualify as rebuttal but, of course, I, or I think it will be Mr. Scott, will deal with matters more fully on Wednesday or Thursday where there is an issue arising.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We ought to have also a time estimate for the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you haven't done it already.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I've proposed that already to Mr. Scott and we'll try and do that. I think we can certainly do it with some. The -- many of the witnesses would be giving evidence on very restricted issues and would not be long and, indeed, I think we've even suggested within the pleading as a possibility, were it to commend itself, that for some of the witnesses, statements recently taken could qualify as evidence in chief if adopted, freeing up time for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice, while you are on your feet, if I understand you correctly, you say that, notwithstanding the decision of the Appeals Chamber, you intend to use affidavits for rebuttal witnesses. Have I understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you think this is compatible with the decision of the Appeals Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We do. Indeed, we don't think that, as presently formulated, Rule 94 ter necessarily contemplates evidence in rebuttal and therefore one has to look at another route for the admission of affidavit evidence, but we take the view that this will be a proper, helpful, useful, and fair method for adducing evidence in certain circumstances, thus our document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. President, we will be addressing that particular point in our rebuttal opposition. We urge the Court to look carefully at the Appeals Chamber decision because we think that it's completely inconsistent with the proposal made by the Prosecution, but we can -- we'll outline that in our pleadings. As I said, that should be ready for tomorrow. I did forget, there is one more outstanding issue, that's the day late and dollar short issue, our request for a binding order for the Kingdom of Sweden.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That, I can tell you, is at hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, we'll sit again on Wednesday, then, since that's the earliest available date to deal with these matters. Half past nine Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
